lessons.title: Animal tissues, organs and organ systems
lessons.summary: Tour the digestive system and its enzymes, the heart, blood vessels and blood, then look at coronary heart disease, lifestyle risk factors and cancer.
objectives: I can describe how enzymes digest carbohydrates, proteins and lipids and explain the lock-and-key model.
I can describe the structure of the heart and the three types of blood vessel and relate them to their functions.
I can describe the components of blood and their jobs.
I can evaluate treatments for coronary heart disease.
I can explain how lifestyle risk factors are linked to non-communicable diseases including cancer.

activities.title: Digestion and enzymes
activities.content:
## Breaking food down

Food contains large, insoluble molecules such as starch, protein and fat. They are far too big to pass through the wall of the gut into the blood, so the **digestive system** breaks them into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed. This job is done by **enzymes**: proteins that act as biological catalysts, speeding up reactions without being used up.

Each enzyme has an **active site** with a specific shape. Only one type of substrate fits, like a key fitting a lock. This is the **lock-and-key model**.

| Enzyme | Breaks down | Into | Made in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Carbohydrase (e.g. amylase) | Starch | Sugars (glucose) | Salivary glands, pancreas, small intestine |
| Protease | Proteins | Amino acids | Stomach, pancreas, small intestine |
| Lipase | Lipids (fats) | Fatty acids and glycerol | Pancreas, small intestine |

The products are absorbed in the small intestine and used by cells to build new carbohydrates, proteins and lipids. Some glucose is used in respiration to release energy.

activities.title: Temperature, pH and bile
activities.content:
## Why enzymes need the right conditions

Enzymes work fastest at their **optimum** temperature and pH. Move away from the optimum and the rate of reaction drops.

- Raising the temperature makes molecules move faster so there are more collisions, up to a point.
- Above about 40 °C in humans, the bonds holding the enzyme's shape start to break. The active site changes shape, the substrate no longer fits, and the enzyme is **denatured**. This is permanent.
- Each enzyme also has an optimum pH. Protease in the stomach works best in acid (about pH 2) because the stomach makes hydrochloric acid. Enzymes in the small intestine prefer a slightly alkaline pH.

### Bile

**Bile** is made in the **liver**, stored in the **gall bladder** and released into the small intestine. It does two things:

1. It is **alkaline**, so it neutralises the acid arriving from the stomach, giving intestinal enzymes their optimum pH.
2. It **emulsifies** fats, breaking large droplets into many tiny ones. This increases the surface area for lipase to act on, so fat digestion is faster.

Bile contains no enzymes, so it does not chemically digest fat by itself.

question.text: A student heats a solution of amylase to 70 °C, cools it, then adds starch. No sugar is produced. Explain why.
question.hint: What happened to the shape of the enzyme at 70 °C, and is that reversible?
question.explanation: At 70 °C the amylase was denatured: the active site changed shape permanently, so starch can no longer fit and the reaction cannot happen even after cooling.

markScheme.criterion: Enzyme was denatured at the high temperature
Active site changed shape so substrate (starch) no longer fits

activities.title: The heart
activities.content:
## A double pump

The **heart** is an organ made mostly of muscle that pumps blood around the body. It has **four chambers**: two small upper chambers called **atria** and two larger, thicker lower chambers called **ventricles**.

Blood follows this route:

1. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the **right atrium** through the **vena cava**.
2. It passes into the **right ventricle**, which pumps it through the **pulmonary artery** to the lungs.
3. Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the **pulmonary vein** into the **left atrium**.
4. It passes into the **left ventricle**, which pumps it out through the **aorta** to the rest of the body.

Because blood passes through the heart twice per circuit (once to the lungs, once to the body), this is a **double circulatory system**.

The **left ventricle** has a much thicker muscular wall than the right, because it must push blood all the way around the body rather than just to the nearby lungs. **Valves** between the chambers and at the exits stop blood flowing backwards.

The heart muscle itself is supplied with oxygen by the **coronary arteries**, which branch from the aorta.

The natural resting heart rate is set by a group of cells in the right atrium that act as a **pacemaker**. If this fails, an **artificial pacemaker** (a small electrical device) can be fitted to correct an irregular heartbeat.

activities.title: Worked example: reading a heart diagram
activities.content:
**A diagram shows the heart from the front. Which side is which?**

Remember that diagrams show the heart as if you are looking at the patient. So the patient's **left** side appears on the **right** of the page.

```
        [ from body ]      [ from lungs ]
         vena cava         pulmonary vein
              |                  |
      RIGHT ATRIUM         LEFT ATRIUM
              |                  |
      RIGHT VENTRICLE      LEFT VENTRICLE  (thick wall)
              |                  |
      pulmonary artery          aorta
        [ to lungs ]          [ to body ]
```

**Question:** Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the right?

**Answer:** The left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body, so it needs to generate a higher pressure. The right ventricle only pumps to the lungs, which are close by, so a lower pressure is enough.

**Tip:** Arteries always carry blood *away* from the heart. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, which is the exception to the rule that arteries carry oxygenated blood.

question.text: Put these structures in the order that blood passes through them, starting from the body.
question.hint: Blood goes to the lungs between the right side and the left side of the heart.
question.explanation: Vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.

activities.title: Blood vessels and blood
activities.content:
## Three kinds of vessel

| Vessel | Carries blood | Wall | Lumen | Other features |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Artery** | Away from the heart at high pressure | Thick, muscular and elastic | Narrow | Elastic fibres stretch and recoil to keep blood moving |
| **Vein** | Back to the heart at low pressure | Thin | Wide | Valves prevent backflow |
| **Capillary** | Between arteries and veins | One cell thick | Very narrow | Short diffusion distance for exchange of substances |

You may be asked to calculate rate of blood flow: **rate = volume ÷ time**.

## What is in blood?

Blood is a tissue made of a liquid, **plasma**, with cells suspended in it.

- **Plasma** transports dissolved substances: carbon dioxide, glucose, urea, hormones and proteins.
- **Red blood cells** carry oxygen. They contain **haemoglobin**, which binds to oxygen in the lungs. They have a **biconcave** shape for a large surface area and **no nucleus** so there is more room for haemoglobin.
- **White blood cells** defend against pathogens by engulfing them (phagocytosis), making antibodies or making antitoxins.
- **Platelets** are cell fragments that help blood **clot** at a wound.

question.text: Which features of arteries help them carry blood at high pressure? Select all that apply.
question.hint: High pressure needs strength and the ability to stretch and recoil.
question.explanation: Arteries have thick muscular walls and elastic fibres to cope with and maintain high pressure. Valves and one-cell-thick walls belong to veins and capillaries respectively.

options.text: Elastic fibres that stretch and recoil

options.feedback: Valves are a feature of veins, where pressure is low.
That is a capillary feature for fast diffusion.

question.text: During a test, 1560 cm³ of blood flows through a patient's aorta in 20 seconds. Calculate the rate of blood flow in cm³ per minute.
question.hint: Work out the flow per second first, then multiply to get per minute.
question.explanation: 1560 ÷ 20 = 78 cm³ per second. 78 × 60 = 4680 cm³ per minute.

activities.title: Coronary heart disease and its treatment
activities.content:
## When the heart's own supply is blocked

In **coronary heart disease (CHD)**, layers of fatty material build up inside the **coronary arteries**. The lumen narrows, so less blood reaches the heart muscle. Less oxygen means less respiration, and the muscle can be damaged. A complete blockage causes a heart attack.

CHD is a **non-communicable disease**: it cannot be passed from person to person.

### Treatments

| Treatment | How it helps | Drawbacks |
|---|---|---|
| **Statins** | Drugs that lower blood cholesterol, slowing the build-up of fatty material | Must be taken long term; possible side effects such as muscle pain; effect is not immediate |
| **Stents** | A mesh tube inserted into the narrowed artery to hold it open | Surgery carries a risk; does not stop the disease from continuing elsewhere |
| **Heart valve replacement** | Faulty valves (leaky or stiff) are replaced with **biological** (animal) or **mechanical** valves | Surgery risk; mechanical valves need anti-clotting drugs; biological valves wear out |
| **Heart transplant** | Whole heart replaced with a donor heart when the heart fails | Shortage of donors; risk of rejection; major surgery |
| **Artificial heart** | Mechanical pump used while waiting for a donor or to let the heart rest | Not a permanent solution; risk of blood clots |

When evaluating, weigh the benefit (reduced risk, symptoms relieved) against the risks, cost and how long the treatment lasts.

question.text: Which treatment for coronary heart disease works by holding a narrowed artery open?
question.hint: Think of a small scaffold placed inside the vessel.
question.explanation: A stent is a mesh tube inserted into the artery to keep it open. Statins are drugs that reduce cholesterol.

options.feedback: Statins lower cholesterol; they do not physically widen the artery.
Pacemakers correct the rhythm of the heartbeat.

activities.title: Health, risk factors and cancer
activities.content:
## What affects health?

**Health** is a state of physical and mental well-being. It is affected by diseases, by diet, by stress and by life situations. Diseases can interact:

- A weak immune system makes infections more likely.
- Some viruses living in cells can trigger cancers.
- Immune reactions to a pathogen can trigger allergies such as asthma.
- Severe physical illness can lead to mental illness such as depression.

### Risk factors

A **risk factor** is anything that increases the chance of developing a disease. Some are lifestyle choices, some are substances in the body or environment:

| Risk factor | Linked disease |
|---|---|
| Diet high in fat, lack of exercise, smoking | Cardiovascular disease |
| Obesity | Type 2 diabetes |
| Alcohol | Liver disease and reduced brain function |
| Smoking, alcohol in pregnancy | Harm to the unborn baby |
| Carcinogens such as ionising radiation and tobacco smoke | Cancer |

A risk factor being **correlated** with a disease does not prove it **causes** it, but for many (like smoking and lung cancer) the mechanism is now understood.

### Cancer

Cancer is caused by changes in cells that lead to **uncontrolled growth and division**, forming a **tumour**.

- **Benign** tumours stay in one place, usually inside a membrane, and do not invade other tissues.
- **Malignant** tumours are cancers: cells can break off, travel in the blood and form **secondary tumours** elsewhere.

Risk factors include genetic factors as well as lifestyle.

question.text:
A 58-year-old patient has narrowed coronary arteries. The doctor suggests either statins or a stent.

(a) Explain why narrowed coronary arteries can damage the heart muscle. (2 marks)

(b) Give **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of using statins compared with fitting a stent. (2 marks)

(c) Coronary heart disease is described as non-communicable. What does *non-communicable* mean? (1 mark)
question.hint: For (a), follow the chain: less blood → less oxygen → less respiration. For (b), think about surgery risk versus taking a daily drug.
question.explanation: (a) Less blood flows to the heart muscle, so the muscle cells receive less oxygen for respiration and cannot release enough energy, which can cause a heart attack. (b) Statins avoid the risks of surgery and slow the build-up of fatty material across all arteries, but they must be taken every day for life and can cause side effects, whereas a stent gives an immediate result. (c) Non-communicable means it cannot be spread from one person to another.

markScheme.criterion: Less blood (and therefore less oxygen) reaches the heart muscle
Less respiration / less energy released so cells are damaged or die (heart attack)
Advantage of statins: no surgery/risk of infection, or reduces cholesterol/fatty build-up everywhere
Disadvantage of statins: side effects, must be taken long term/daily, slow to act
Non-communicable means not passed from person to person / not infectious

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Enzymes** are catalysts with a specific active site (lock and key). Amylase → sugars, protease → amino acids, lipase → fatty acids and glycerol. High temperature or wrong pH **denatures** them.
- **Bile** (liver → gall bladder) neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fats.
- The **heart** has four chambers; the left ventricle is thickest; blood passes through twice per circuit (double circulation).
- **Arteries**: thick, elastic, high pressure. **Veins**: thin, valves, low pressure. **Capillaries**: one cell thick for exchange.
- **Blood** = plasma + red cells (haemoglobin) + white cells (defence) + platelets (clotting).
- **CHD**: fatty build-up in coronary arteries; treated with statins, stents, valve replacement, transplants or artificial hearts.
- **Risk factors** (smoking, diet, alcohol, obesity, carcinogens) raise the chance of non-communicable diseases. **Malignant** tumours spread; **benign** ones do not.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: bile contains enzymes that digest fat.
practiceQuestions.hint: Bile helps lipase, but does it do the chemical breakdown itself?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Bile has no enzymes. It emulsifies fat into small droplets and neutralises stomach acid, which helps lipase work faster.

practiceQuestions.text: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygenated blood to the body?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood out through the aorta to the whole body.

options.feedback: The right ventricle pumps to the lungs.

metadata.blanksText: Red blood cells contain ___ which binds to oxygen. ___ are cell fragments that help blood to clot. Dissolved substances such as glucose and urea are carried in the ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: The protein in red cells is red; the fragments are small plates; the liquid part is not water.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Haemoglobin binds oxygen; platelets help clotting; plasma carries dissolved substances.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each blood vessel to its key feature.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Arteries have thick elastic walls; veins have valves; capillaries are one cell thick.

pairs.right: Thick elastic wall to withstand high pressure
Wall one cell thick for rapid exchange

practiceQuestions.text: A patient's heart pumps 70 cm³ of blood with each beat and beats 72 times per minute. Calculate the volume of blood pumped in one minute, in cm³.
practiceQuestions.hint: Volume per minute = volume per beat × beats per minute.

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following are risk factors for cardiovascular disease? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what damages or narrows blood vessels.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Smoking and a diet high in saturated fat both increase the risk of cardiovascular disease. Regular exercise reduces the risk, and ionising radiation is a risk factor for cancer, not CHD.

options.text: A diet high in saturated fat

options.feedback: Radiation is a carcinogen, linked to cancer.

practiceQuestions.text: Describe the difference between a benign tumour and a malignant tumour.
practiceQuestions.hint: One stays put; the other can spread.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A benign tumour stays in one place (often within a membrane) and does not invade other tissues. A malignant tumour is cancerous: cells can break away, travel in the blood and form secondary tumours elsewhere.

markScheme.criterion: Benign tumours stay in one place / do not invade other tissues
Malignant tumours spread to other parts of the body / form secondary tumours

practiceQuestions.text: Put these steps in order to describe how fat is digested in the small intestine.
practiceQuestions.hint: Bile does its job before lipase can work quickly.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bile from the gall bladder emulsifies the fat into small droplets, increasing the surface area; lipase then breaks the fat into fatty acids and glycerol, which are absorbed.
order: Bile is released from the gall bladder into the small intestine
Fat is emulsified into small droplets
Lipase breaks the fat into fatty acids and glycerol
Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the blood

practiceQuestions.text:
A student investigated the effect of pH on the rate at which amylase breaks down starch. They found the reaction was fastest at pH 7 and very slow at pH 2.

(a) Explain, in terms of the enzyme's structure, why the reaction was very slow at pH 2. (2 marks)

(b) Protease in the stomach works best at pH 2. Explain why this is useful and how the small intestine is later returned to a suitable pH for its own enzymes. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: Use the terms *active site* and *denatured* in (a). For (b), which alkaline liquid reaches the small intestine?
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) At pH 2 the amylase is denatured: its active site changes shape, so starch no longer fits and the reaction slows. (b) The stomach produces hydrochloric acid, so a protease with an optimum of pH 2 can work there. Bile, which is alkaline, is released into the small intestine and neutralises the acid so that intestinal enzymes are at their optimum pH.

markScheme.criterion: Active site changes shape so starch (substrate) no longer fits
Stomach contains hydrochloric acid so protease adapted to acidic pH works there
Bile is alkaline and neutralises the acid in the small intestine

practiceQuestions.text: A patient has a faulty heart valve replaced with a mechanical valve. Which of these is a disadvantage of a mechanical valve compared with a biological valve?
practiceQuestions.hint: Metal and plastic surfaces can cause blood to do something unwanted.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Mechanical valves can cause blood clots, so patients must take anti-clotting drugs for life. They generally last longer than biological valves.

options.text: The patient must take anti-clotting drugs for life

options.feedback: Mechanical valves usually last longer than biological ones.

options.text: It cannot be fitted by surgery

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: red blood cells have no nucleus, which leaves more room for haemoglobin.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the adaptations of a red blood cell.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, so more haemoglobin can be packed in, and their biconcave shape gives a large surface area.
